title: Crypto Blackpill
content:
I've been reading some news recently regarding the update on Counter-Strike (CS:GO) skins; to sum up the whole drama in very few words, the market price of those skins crashed following one executive decision, which made some of those rare skins, well, not so rare. I could not help but think how strong of a display it is of the failure of crypto as an industry.

I'm personally not that interested in the video game industry, but I'm curious about internet IP and the way people perceive value. CS:GO skins had been one of the best performing assets these past few years, up until last week, when billions of dollars of value evaporated overnight. 

When you go from a fixed supply asset to a not-so-fixed supply, the market usually tends to react like this:

![image](https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/gh/alexisnsns/pfalexns-posts@main/images/crypto-blackpill/1761335309555-Screenshot%202025-10-24%20at%2015.47.59.png)
source: https://esportfire.com/indexes

This crash can be attributed to the very structure of the market; it relied on a centralized entity which could set the rules without any consultation or counterparty. This should not really come of as a surprise (but then why would people spend so much money in a market where the platform can pull the rug from under you at any moment), but it still raises an interesting point, which is **the issue of reproductibility in the age of the internet**. I think this question is central to explaining why so many people invest so much time working in the industry of globally distributed, permisionless, decentralized ledgers, aka. crypto.

In my opinion, this CS:GO debacle perfectly encapsulates the need for **permisionless property rights on the internet**, and how simple web3 implementations could have saved these gamers/investors portfolios. 

In this specific case, it's not too far-fetched to think that skins could have taken the form of a collection of non-fungible tokens from the beginning (or a similar technical implementation, we'll stick to NFTs as it is the most easily understandable one):  first and foremost to 

1/ Preserve their value by making dilution impossible (users invested time/money to get them). Smart contracts make it so that once deployed on a blockchain, there is no way, even for insiders, to edit the supply of a given asset.

2/ Make them tradeable *outside the franchise*, between platforms (eg. use your CS skins in another platform like Call Of Duty, sell them on OpenSea, whatever), which would reduce some of the issues of vendor lock-in. 

It is very depressing to see that blockchain tech is not even used in those specific situtations where it has an obvious edge, so one can ask what do we even have to show for it, ten years after the first smart contracts were rolled out.

### Crypto has definitely found -at least some- PMF

Some cool things have been built in these past ten years.

- (1) Non reproducible content native to the internet. It certainly hasn't found a mainstream audience yet, but the cheapest items of the most iconic collection still trade for more than 150k dollars a piece, 8 years after their creation (cryptoPunks). Honestly, the fact that NFT's have even 1 dollar of marketcap is in itself quite revolutionary and has plenty of interesting ramifications regarding what the internet of value is and could be. 

- (2) Stablecoins; instant money transfer in a non-hyperinflationary currency across-borders + ability to save in hard currencies (or at least harder than their local ones) like CHF/USD for people in hyperinflationary regimes like Turkish/Argentinian people. I think that's the biggest achievement yet, which is of course quite ironic considering crypto was supposed to replace, not extend, the current monetary system and dollar hegemony.

- (3) Decentralized voting with proof-of-ownership; think DAOs, futarchy, etc.

- (4) Permisionless databases; write a poem on an Ethereum bloc. It'll be visible to anyone with an internet connection and can't be taken down. In human history, there is nothing that comes even remotely close to this.

- (5) Prediction markets; Polymarket has been the huge success of this cycle; permissionless betting; opens the door to an infinite amount of crazy experimentations and insider trading, but definitely found PMF. 

- (6) Store of value in non seizable assets. Even if BTC has been lagging so much behind gold in Q4 25, when I write this post (why not simply save in tokenized gold like XAUT then?), tens of thousands of people save in Bitcoin, which can't be ignored ('why would I trade a hard, finite currency for one they print out of thin air?'). I'm personally a heavy bitcoin critic but its definitely here to stay, at this point.

### Ruins all around

It seems however that massive, absolutely massive amounts of resources (human attention, talent, and financial capital) have been spent on crypto with very little to show for it in what amounts to look like a negative sum game. 

The industry seems to be heading in two main directions now, which are both a disappointment to me.

1/ The 24/7 casino. I'm all for experimentation (this being the very idea behind a *permisionless* technology), but hyper-gambling is a net negative here. Small investors are being slaughtered on memecoins; people spend an insane amount of time looking at charts and commenting them. The current meta -perp dexes- is just an extension of the casino. There is no value creation here, just extraction.

2/ The more 'serious' side of crypto, on the other hand, is just trying to put TradFi on-chain. It's more interesting, but people did not join crypto just to have US dollars on a blockchain.

Overall, it's a pretty bleak landscape outside of some niche projects and moonshot teams (the whole ZK push, RailGun privacy pools, Gnosis VPN...).

### What -still- excites me about the industry

Plenty of stuff remains to be built, in some wildly different areas. 

- Proof of Humanity. With the rise of agentic AI, we'll need to have a way to prove humanity on the Internet. Small cognitive tasks like Captcha are completely outdated as of 2025, as there seems to be a growing overlap between the most advanced AI tools and the individuals with the least cognitive ability on the Internet. I don't have an answer for this (yet), as most solutions so far raise massive privacy concerns (eg. worldCoin). I think tying a SIWE to a wallet with at least some monetary value in there would be some short term solution, as it would dramatically raise the cost of spamming. The implementation could be fairly basic; you can't post on a forum if you haven't done a SIWE on a wallet with at least 0.1 ETH on mainnet.

- Privacy preserving stablecoins; stablecoins is a topic in which I'm very interested. So far, what we have is basically a replica of the fiat system with faster settlement and less privacy. We can do better than that; I'm not even sure the solution will come from stablecoins per se, probably more at the chain layer, with privacy preserving transactions (think ZK).

- A proper **non-volatile** internet-native store of value, non pegged to fiat. I was drawn to crypto for the main cypherpunk proposition of separation of the state and money. Permisionless, decentralized, private money, with currency competition. This was I think the most promising use case for crypto (being born in the aftermath of 2008) and of course the idea behind Satoshi's whitepaper. The small-block won in the blockwars, BTC was reduced to a digital gold, and so far other true permisionless competitors such as ETH are not used as units of exchange. Stablecoins seem to have won. It's already something, but it is still custodial, except for some like RAI, which as always Vitalik puts in great words, calling this “a low-volatility asset without relying on banks”, which is actually the end-game, I think, and what the industry should be working towards.

- A bit of a contrarian take but I still think that NFTs have potential. People want to signal in-group membership. Having fixed supply profile pictures, for example, makes for interesting internet native cultures to emerge (see Milady) 

- I feel like there is room for a properly decentralized social network. Farcaster is trying to fill this niche, but it is still too crypto-centric. 


I still think there are some things to be proud of here, and some things to look forward to. The Trump family is burning to the ground the last remnants of credibility we had as an industry, but I'm confident we'll manage to save at least a few good ideas from the ashes, and we'll rebuild from there. Bitcoin is often compared to a cockroach, chugging along blocks every 10 minutes or so, whatever happens in the outside world. As developers and cryptocurrency enthusiasts, we might want to replicate this attitude for the next few years.
